title: Disturbing building fabric: asbestos, lead and silica when drilling and coring
verdict: I would not sign this and I would not send a crew out on it. It is the best-drafted statement in the set and its law is genuinely sound — I pulled the primary sources and checked them line by line. WHS Reg s 291(a),(d),(f),(k),(o) read exactly as quoted; s 419(3) and s 419(5) (which does name AS 4964:2004), s 422(2)(b), s 423(2), s 446(1)/(3)/(4), s 447(1)(a)/(2), s 448, ss 485-489, s 79(3), s 299(2)(d) and the s 299(4) fall-controls-considered rule, and the whole silica chain — s 529B(1)(b) five-control list, s 529B(3) naming AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS 1715:2009, s 529BA, s 529CA(1),(1A),(2)(d)-(f),(3),(5), s 529CB(2) and the s 529CB(3) SWMS-as-plan carve-out — all say what the document says they say. The Electrical Safety Regulation 2013 has been correctly replaced throughout: I read SL 2026 No. 113 as made, and s 136, s 139(3)(a) (portable safety switch tested by pushing the test button immediately after connection), s 140(2) (AS/NZS 3012), part 8 division 3 with s 193 defining "near" as within 3m of an exposed energised part, s 195, s 196(1) and (2)(a), s 197, s 198 and s 199 are all real and all accurately paraphrased. The wet-coring conflict with the live-equipment hold has been fixed by explicit two-way cross-reference between steps[3] and steps[7], the silica step honestly refuses to claim a low residual, the locator and the GPR survey are correctly demoted to administrative with the reasoning written out, and there is a fire-while-isolated emergency response. That is real work and it should be said. But being right about the statute is not the same as controlling the room, and four things in this document will hurt somebody. steps[3].hazards[2] names "Sprinkler pipe, gas line, hydraulic riser or comms behind the sheet" and then not one of the eight controls in that step touches hydraulic or gas services — the only detection offered is a cable and rebar locator, which finds neither, and the emergency section has no response for a struck gas or charged pipe at all, in a document that expressly sends technicians to drill ceilings in hospitals and day surgeries where medical gas copper runs in exactly that void. steps[1].hazards[3] names friable pipe lagging in the riser you are drilling beside, and every asbestos control in the document keys off drilling INTO asbestos: the stop rule fires on the substrate at the drill point and step 7 fires only when "You cut into it", so a technician can hammer-drill 300mm from registered friable lagging with nothing in the statement telling them to stop. Drilling switchboard and FIP backing is put in scope by whenRequired and named in steps[1].hazards[1], yet the only electrical control is isolating "a circuit in the drill zone" — which leaves a board's incomer, busbars and terminations live millimetres behind the panel you are drilling — and arc flash appears nowhere. And in a statement whose whole job is putting a person hard up against a ceiling on a platform, crush between the basket and the overhead structure is never named and never controlled, on either a boom lift or the scissor lift the document actively steers you toward. Any one of the first three is the same fault that failed the other five: a hazard the paper names and then leaves standing. Fix the four fatals, the platform-ladder allowance and the stale-register gap, add noise and heat to the steps, and correct steps[10].residualRisk, and I would read it again.

blocking.problem: steps[3].hazards[2] names "Sprinkler pipe, gas line, hydraulic riser or comms behind the sheet" and no control in the step addresses any of them. The eight controls cover concealed electrical cable, post-tensioned tendons, reinforcement and wet-slurry tracking only. The nearest thing is steps[3].controls[5], "Scan the full drill footprint with a cable and rebar locator, two passes at 90 degrees" — a cable and rebar locator does not find copper or polymer hydraulic pipe, a plastic sprinkler drop, or a gas line, and the control's own honesty paragraph about false negatives is written only about cables. Nothing requires hydraulic or gas services drawings, nothing requires a charged line to be drained or a gas line depressurised, and the emergency section has no entry for a struck pipe or gas line — its seven headings are asbestos, cable strike/shock, fall, first aid, working alone, eye injury, fire while isolated, and cut tendon. This matters most where the document itself sends the crew: permits[7] and steps[4].controls[3] put technicians into hospitals, day surgeries and aged care, where medical gas copper (oxygen, nitrous oxide, medical air) runs in the ceiling void detectors mount into. A rotary hammer through an oxygen line in an enclosed void is a fire; through a gas line it is an explosion; through a charged hydrant or sprinkler main it is high-pressure water into a room the document elsewhere says may contain live switchgear. The hrcw array also omits the two paragraphs that this hazard triggers: I confirmed against legislation.qld.gov.au that WHS Reg s 291(i) is "is carried out on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping" and s 291(j) is "is carried out on or near chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines".
blocking.fix: Insert as the new steps[3].controls[1], level "eliminate", immediately after the existing isolation-first control: "Get the site's hydraulic, medical gas and fuel gas services drawings alongside the electrical drawings, and move the drill point clear of any charged pipework — sprinkler, hydrant, hydraulic riser, natural gas, LPG, oxygen, nitrous oxide or medical air. A pipe you do not drill cannot be struck, and no locator on this job finds them." Insert as the new steps[3].controls[4], level "isolate", after the wet-drilling hold: "Where a gas or medical gas line may run in the drill zone and the point cannot be moved, the line is isolated at the valve, depressurised and proven by the site or its gas fitter before the bit touches the surface, and the isolation is locked and tagged. Charged sprinkler, hydrant or hydraulic pipework in the drill zone is isolated and drained by the site's fire or hydraulic contractor, or the point moves. Percussion drilling near live gas does not proceed on a scan." Amend steps[3].controls[5] to add: "A cable and rebar locator finds neither pipework nor gas lines — for services other than cable and rebar the drawings and the site's hydraulic and mechanical contractors are the only source, and where they cannot confirm, the point moves." Add to hrcw: {"clause":"Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(i)","text":"Construction work that is carried out on or near pressurised gas distribution mains or piping"} and {"clause":"Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld), s 291(j)","text":"Construction work that is carried out on or near chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines"}. Add to emergency: "STRUCK A GAS OR MEDICAL GAS LINE. Stop, leave the tool where it is, do not withdraw the bit and do not operate any switch, light or radio. Get everyone out and upwind, prop nothing, kill no power at a switch inside the area. Call 000 and the site's gas contractor from outside the area, and have the site isolate at the meter or the zone valve. Do not re-enter until they say the atmosphere is clear. An uncontrolled escape of gas is a dangerous incident under Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 37(c), and an uncontrolled escape of a pressurised substance under s 37(d) — call WHSQ on 1300 362 128. STRUCK A CHARGED SPRINKLER, HYDRANT OR HYDRAULIC LINE. Get clear and get everyone out of the space below. Have the building manager shut the isolation valve and record the time — the system is now impaired and that goes on the permit and to the fire safety adviser. Treat every wetted surface and anything below as a live electrical hazard until an electrician clears it, and do not go back to the hole until the line is drained."

blocking.problem: steps[1].hazards[3] names "Friable pipe lagging in the riser you are drilling beside" and nothing in the document controls it. Every asbestos control keys off drilling INTO asbestos, not beside it. steps[1].controls[0] stops the job only where the point itself is suspect — "A point that is not clearly on non-ACM substrate in the register does not get drilled today" — so a drill point on sound concrete 300mm from registered friable lagging passes that test. steps[6] fires only on "You cut into it and it is, or might be, asbestos". steps[0].controls[1] asks you to "Note every ACM entry within 5 m of a planned drill point, its recorded condition" — noting is not controlling, and the document is elsewhere scrupulous about that distinction (it says so itself at steps[3].controls[6] and steps[11].controls[0]). Percussive hammer drilling, the vibration it puts into a riser, the air movement it creates and the H-class vacuum's exhaust all release fibres from degraded lagging without anyone touching it, and the crew's only protection is a P2 half-face they believe is a backstop. The document's own risk key calls the outcome catastrophic (mesothelioma), and steps[6].controls[3] correctly says friable material is class A work "at any quantity, however small, with no area threshold" — but only once you have cut it.
blocking.fix: Insert as the new steps[1].controls[1], level "eliminate", directly after the mark-and-photograph stop rule: "Friable ACM in the same space stops the drill even where the drill point is clean. Where the register records, or the tells show, friable material — pipe or boiler lagging, sprayed limpet, vermiculite, millboard — anywhere in the riser, shaft, plant room or void you are drilling into, the drill point moves out of that enclosure. Percussion, vibration, air movement and vacuum exhaust release fibres from friable material without a bit ever touching it, and the stop rule in step 7 will not save you because you will not have cut anything. Noting it under step 1 is not controlling it." Insert as the new steps[1].controls[2], level "isolate": "If the fixing cannot be relocated out of the enclosure, the work does not proceed until the site has had the friable material removed or fully encapsulated by a class A licensed removalist, with air monitoring by a licensed asbestos assessor and a clearance certificate under Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) ss 473 and 474. That is a separate job on a separate SWMS — call the supervisor, and leave the riser shut." Also amend steps[0].controls[1] to read "...and where any of those entries within 5 m is friable, the job does not start until step 2's friable rule has been applied by the supervisor."

blocking.field: whenRequired ("or switchboard backing"); steps[1].hazards[1]; steps[3].controls[0] and [1]; permits[2]; emergency ("CABLE STRIKE OR ELECTRIC SHOCK")
blocking.problem: The document puts drilling into switchboard backing squarely in scope — whenRequired opens "Any time you put a bit into a wall, ceiling, slab, riser or switchboard backing in a building built before 1990" — and steps[1].hazards[1] names "AC sheet used as the switchboard backing panel behind the fire panel". It then treats that substrate purely as an asbestos question (Zelemite and Ausbestos are in the tells list at steps[1].controls[1]) and never as an electrical one. Every electrical control in the statement is written about a circuit passing through the fabric: steps[3].controls[0] says "Where a live circuit runs through the drill zone and cannot be avoided, do not drill until it is dead"; steps[3].controls[1] has the electrician isolate "at the board that feeds the area"; permits[2] is an isolation permit "where a circuit in the drill zone must be de-energised". None of that makes a board backing panel safe. The incoming submain, the busbars, the main switch terminals and the outgoing terminations sit directly behind that panel and stay live when the sub-circuit feeding the room is locked off — the crew will have followed every control in step 4 to the letter and still be driving a rotary hammer into an energised busbar. The consequence is a phase-to-phase fault and arc flash, and arc flash appears nowhere in the document: the emergency section's "CABLE STRIKE OR ELECTRIC SHOCK" paragraph is written for a shock through the body ("Treat for burns at both entry and exit") and has nothing for flash burn, blast or eye injury from an arc.
blocking.fix: Insert as the new steps[3].controls[0], level "eliminate", ahead of everything else in the step: "Nothing is drilled into, through, or into the wall directly behind, a switchboard, distribution board, MSB, FIP, ASE or sub-board enclosure or its backing panel. Detector bases, brackets and cable supports do not land on board backing — move the fixing onto wall structure clear of the enclosure and record the offset and the reason. Isolating the sub-circuit that feeds the area does NOT make a board backing panel safe: the incoming submain, the busbars and the terminations behind it stay live. If a fixing genuinely must be made to the board, the whole board is isolated at its supply and proven de-energised at the point of work by the site's licensed electrician (Electrical Safety Regulation 2026 (Qld) s 196(1), and s 196(2)(a) — each exposed part is treated as energised until it is isolated and found not to be), locked open under your own personal danger lock with a warning sign (s 198). If the board cannot be shut down, the work is electrical work on or near energised equipment under part 8 division 3, needs the recorded risk assessment and separate energised-work SWMS under s 199, and does not proceed on this document." Add to the emergency "CABLE STRIKE OR ELECTRIC SHOCK" paragraph: "ARC FLASH AT A BOARD. If a tool has faulted phase-to-phase or phase-to-earth inside or behind a board, do not approach the board and do not attempt to open it. Get the person clear only if you can do it without touching them or the board, kill the supply upstream, and call 000. Treat for flash burn and blast — burns will be worse than they look, and eyes and hearing are both at risk even where the person is walking and talking. The board stays isolated and out of service until a licensed electrician has inspected and cleared it, and nobody re-energises it to check. This is a dangerous incident under Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 37(b) and s 37(e) — call WHSQ on 1300 362 128 and preserve the scene under s 39."

blocking.field: steps[5].hazards (all 7) and steps[5].controls; emergency ("FALL FROM THE PLATFORM OR THE EWP")
blocking.problem: steps[5] is the access step for work whose entire purpose is putting a person's head and shoulders up against a ceiling or slab soffit, and it never names crush or entrapment between the platform and the structure overhead. The seven hazards cover falls, snatch, dropped tools, core plugs, an unanchored stand, "EWP driven into sprinkler heads or services" and suspension in a harness — not the operator's own body pinned between the top rail or the control panel and the soffit, beam, duct or pipe run above, which is how most EWP operators are killed. There is no crush-prevention or secondary-guarding requirement anywhere: no pressure-sensing bar or plate, no trigger-guarded control, no rule about how the up control is operated when the basket is close to the structure, no rule about setting the platform height so the drill point is at chest height rather than directly over the controls. The gap is worse than it looks because steps[5].controls[5] actively steers the crew to the machine with no rescue plan attached — "No second person, no boom lift: use a scissor lift, a mobile scaffold or a platform" — and crush against overhead structure kills scissor-lift operators too, while every ground-rescue provision in the document (steps[5].controls[5], the emergency fall paragraph's "The second person lowers the basket from the ground controls") is written for boom-type EWPs only. The emergency section has no entry for a trapped or crushed operator, and an operator pinned against a soffit generally cannot reach their own controls or breathe.
blocking.fix: Insert as the new steps[5].controls[3], level "engineering", between the guardrailed-platform control and the side-handle control: "Overhead crush. On this work the drill point is above the platform, so the basket is by definition close to the structure. Set the platform height so the drill point is at chest to head height and not directly above the control panel, and position it so no part of you can be trapped between the top rail, the controls or the basket floor and the slab soffit, beams, ductwork or pipe runs above. A boom-type EWP used for overhead drilling has its secondary guarding — crush-prevention bar, sensing plate or trigger-guarded control — fitted, functional and proved at pre-start; a machine without it is not used for overhead work. Raise in short bursts, hand clear of the up control between bursts, eyes on the overhead clearance not on the ceiling grid. Stop the machine before you look up, lean out or reposition your body, and never raise while your torso is between the controls and the structure." Add to emergency, before FIRST AID COVER: "TRAPPED OR CRUSHED IN A PLATFORM. Do not wait for the operator to free themselves — a person pinned against the structure often cannot reach the controls or draw breath. The person on the ground brings the platform straight down on the ground controls, or on the emergency lowering or descent valve if the ground controls are dead, then calls 000. Do not raise the platform to relieve the pressure. Support the person and keep them still until the ambulance arrives, and leave the machine where it stops. This is why nobody drills overhead off a platform alone — the ground person is the rescue, on a scissor lift as much as on a boom lift." Also amend steps[5].responsible to read "...with a second competent person on the ground for any boom-type EWP work and for any overhead drilling or coring from a platform".

blocking.problem: steps[5].controls[2] permits a platform ladder as an equivalent to a guardrailed platform for this work: "Work off a platform with guardrails — scissor lift, mobile scaffold or a platform ladder with a handrail." That contradicts the two hazards immediately above it in the same step: steps[5].hazards[0] "Fall above 2 m with both hands on a rotary hammer overhead" and steps[5].hazards[1] "Drill snatch or bit bind pushing you off the platform". A platform ladder has a front handrail, not guardrails on all sides, and it cannot hold a person against a lateral snatch when both hands are on a rotary hammer above shoulder height with no free hand for support. The control correctly rules out "a leaning A-frame" and then lets the platform ladder in beside a scissor lift as though they were the same class of protection, which is exactly the reading a technician standing in a plant room at 7am will take.
blocking.fix: Amend steps[5].controls[2] to open: "Work off a guardrailed platform — scissor lift or mobile scaffold — for any overhead rotary hammer or coring work, and for any work above 2 m. A platform ladder with a handrail is used only below 2 m, only for short-duration single-handed work with one hand free on the rail, and never for two-handed overhead hammer drilling: the snatch hazard named above in this step is the one thing it cannot hold you against. A rotary hammer overhead off a leaning A-frame is not a control at all." Leave the rest of the control (the s 299(4) and s 79 wording and the scaffolding licence threshold) unchanged.

blocking.problem: steps[0].hazards[1] names "Register exists but was last reviewed before the refurbishment that put the ceiling in" and none of the six controls in the step tells the crew what to do about it. controls[0] deals with there being no register at all, controls[1] with reading it for ACM entries and inaccessible or not-inspected areas, controls[3] with confirming the construction date, controls[4] with there being no register, controls[5] with scope growth. A register that exists, is signed and is simply out of date passes every one of them, and it is the most common failure mode in the field: the register describes the fabric that was there in 2006, the ceiling was replaced in 2014, and the crew drills believing they are covered. The document has the tool and does not use it — WHS Reg s 448 is in references but is cited in no control; I confirmed its text, which requires the person with management or control to ensure that before demolition or refurbishment the asbestos register is reviewed and, if inadequate having regard to the proposed work, revised.
blocking.fix: Insert as the new steps[0].controls[2], level "administrative", after the read-the-register control: "Check the register's last review date against the building's own history, and ask the site directly what has been refurbished since. Where a fitout, a re-ceiling, a new riser or any other refurbishment postdates the review, the register does not describe the fabric you are about to drill, and a stale register is not a register for that area. Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 448 requires the person with management or control to ensure that, before refurbishment is carried out, the asbestos register is reviewed and, if it is inadequate having regard to the proposed work, revised — ask for that review in writing and get the revised register before the job is booked. Until it exists, every drill point in the refurbished area is treated as asbestos under the Safe QLD rule and the job does not start."

blocking.problem: steps[10] ("Make the penetration good") is rated initialRisk "high", residualRisk "low", and that is unsupportable on the document's own published key. whenRequired sets out the grid explicitly and says consequence is rated "for the outcome of THAT STEP failing, on the footing that the later steps in this SWMS are still standing between you and the worst case". The only later step is steps[11], which restores detection and files paperwork — nothing there catches a bad fire-stop. The outcome of this step failing is the hazard the step itself names: "A cored hole through a fire-rated wall or slab left open or packed with loose rockwool, defeating the compartment for the life of the building". That is catastrophic on their own consequence scale (multiple deaths in a fire, and the defect is invisible for decades). Their own grid gives catastrophic a floor of "medium" even at likelihood "rare", and "high" at "unlikely". "Low" is not reachable for this step by any row of the grid, and a low residual on the one step that reinstates passive fire protection invites a crew to treat it as the tidy-up rather than the work.
blocking.fix: Change steps[10].residualRisk from "low" to "medium" — rare likelihood against a catastrophic consequence, which is what the key produces. If the intent was to reflect that a tested and certified system genuinely restores the compartment, say so in steps[10].controls[0] rather than in the rating: append "A correctly installed tested system restores the FRL, but the consequence of getting it wrong is a compartment breach for the life of the building, so this step never rates below medium — that is why the photographs and the batch record in the next control are mandatory, not optional."

blocking.problem: Noise appears nowhere in any of the twelve steps. Rotary hammering and core drilling in a hard-surfaced plant room is well over the 85 dB(A) eight-hour exposure standard and percussion exceeds the 140 dB(C) peak, and the whole apparatus for it exists in the document — ppe[2] selects protection per AS/NZS 1269.3, references cites ss 56, 57 and 58, training[3] books the audiometric testing — but it is never named as a hazard in the step where the noise is made (steps[7], "Drill and core concrete, brick, block and render"), so no control at any level of the hierarchy is ever applied to it. The crew reads down steps[7].hazards, sees silica, overhead dust, dry coring, vibration and respirator seal, and never sees noise; the only response the document offers is a pair of earmuffs listed four screens away in the PPE array. There is no tool-selection control, no control keeping other people out of the noise area rather than issuing them plugs, and nothing linking the noise to the point ppe[2] itself raises — that over-protection stops you hearing the evacuation alarm in a building whose detection you have just isolated.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[7].hazards: "Noise — rotary hammering and coring in a hard-surfaced plant room or riser runs well above the 85 dB(A) eight-hour exposure standard and, on percussion, above the 140 dB(C) peak (Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 56). The loss is cumulative, permanent and painless while it is happening." Insert as the new steps[7].controls[3], level "engineering", after the vibration control: "Pick the quieter tool and the quieter method. Wet coring on a stand is markedly quieter than hand-held percussion — where either will do the job, core. Keep bits sharp, and shut the plant room door or screen the opening so the noise stays in the space you are in." Insert as the new steps[7].controls[4], level "administrative": "Keep other people out of the noise area rather than handing them hearing protection, and tell the fire watch and anyone working nearby before you start. Wear the protection selected in the PPE list — no more than that, because detection in this area is isolated and you have to be able to hear the alarm raised by voice and the spotter on the ground controls. Audiometric testing under Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) s 58 is booked within 3 months of a worker starting this kind of work and at least every 2 years, before the work, not after."

blocking.problem: Heat illness is never named or controlled, in a statement that mandates the exact combination that causes it. ppe[3] requires "Type 5 Category III disposable coveralls, no external pockets, cuffs taped, where any ACM is present or assumed" and ppe[0] a P2 half-face worn clean-shaven at the seal; the work is overhead physical exertion with a rotary hammer, in Queensland, in plant rooms, roof spaces and ceiling voids where the document has often just had the HVAC shut down (steps[4].controls[4]). A taped non-breathable coverall stops evaporative cooling entirely and the respirator means the technician cannot drink without breaking the seal and leaving the area. There is no work-rest cycle, no hydration provision, no rule about getting out of the suit between holes, nobody tasked with watching for confusion or cramps, and no heat entry in the emergency section — which has responses for asbestos, shock, falls, eyes and fire but not for the technician who goes quiet in the ceiling void at 1pm in February.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[7].hazards: "Heat illness — taped Type 5 coveralls and a P2 half-face during overhead exertion in a Queensland plant room, roof space or ceiling void, often with the HVAC shut down for this job. No evaporative cooling, no way to drink without breaking the seal, and confusion arrives before the person knows anything is wrong." Insert as the new steps[7].controls[3], level "engineering": "Cool the work, not the worker: a portable fan or spot cooling set up outside the containment, the HVAC left running wherever it is not the zone you had shut down, and the hottest work booked for the start of the day where the site allows it." Insert as the new steps[7].controls[7], level "administrative": "Set a work-rest cycle before the first hole and hold to it — out of the coveralls, out of the mask, out of the space, in the shade with water at fixed intervals, shortened as the day heats up. Water is on the job, not in the ute. The second person watches for cramps, headache, confusion, clumsiness or a technician who has stopped sweating, and calls it — the person suffering heat illness is the last one to notice. Nobody works in taped coveralls in a plant room alone." Add to emergency: "HEAT ILLNESS. Stop the work, get them out of the space, coveralls and respirator off, and cool them actively — cold water on the skin, fanning, ice packs to neck, armpits and groin. Give fluids only if they are fully alert. Confusion, agitation, collapse or hot dry skin is heat stroke: call 000 immediately and keep cooling while you wait. Do not send them home to sleep it off and do not let them drive."

blocking.field: hrcw[3]; whenRequired ("CONFINED SPACES — WHAT THIS SWMS DOES NOT AUTHORISE"); steps[1]
blocking.problem: The document claims WHS Reg s 291(f) — "Construction work that is carried out in or near a confined space" — as one of its five HRCW triggers, and handles it entirely in the whenRequired prose. The stop rule is well written and the schedule 19 paraphrase is accurate (I checked it), but it lives in a block of text a technician reads once at induction and never again, and no step carries it. There is no confined space hazard in any of the twelve steps and no control at any level. The consequence is that the determination never gets made at the point where it matters — steps[1] is the arrival walk-around, and it is silent. It also leaves the partial-entry case uncontrolled: nothing tells a technician not to put their head, shoulders or arm through a riser door or a pit opening to mark a point, steady a bit, catch a core plug or retrieve a dropped tool, which is the way people are overcome in shafts on jobs exactly like this one.
blocking.fix: Add to steps[1].hazards: "The riser, shaft, ceiling space, pit or duct at the drill point may be a confined space under Work Health and Safety Regulation 2011 (Qld) schedule 19 — and nothing on this job authorises entering one." Insert as the new steps[1].controls[1], level "eliminate": "Make the confined space call at the opening, on the day, before anything is set up. If the riser, shaft, pit, duct or ceiling space is an enclosed or partially enclosed space not intended primarily to be occupied and is or is likely to be a risk from unsafe oxygen level, airborne contaminants, fire or explosion, or engulfment, the drilling stops there — that is schedule 19 and the whenRequired section of this SWMS. No part of you goes past the opening: not your head, not your shoulders, not an arm to mark a point, steady a bit, catch a core plug or pick up a dropped tool. If the work cannot be done standing outside the opening, it does not get done today. Call the supervisor: entry needs the confined space SWMS, an entry permit under s 67, atmospheric testing, a standby person and rehearsed rescue under s 74, and none of that is on this truck."

blocking.field: emergency ("FALL FROM THE PLATFORM OR THE EWP", final sentence)
blocking.problem: The emergency section states: "A fall, or the release from a height of any plant, substance or thing, is a dangerous incident under Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 37(f)". I checked s 37 against legislation.qld.gov.au: paragraph (f) is "the fall or release from a height of any plant, substance or thing". A person is not plant, a substance or a thing, so a person's fall is not caught by s 37(f). The correct route for an injured worker is s 36 (serious injury or illness — immediate treatment as an in-patient in a hospital, or immediate treatment for a serious head injury, spinal injury, serious burn, amputation, loss of a bodily function or serious lacerations), which makes it notifiable under s 35, and the document's fall paragraph never mentions s 36 or s 35. This is the one citation in the statement that says something other than what the section says, and every other one I checked was accurate. It will not injure anybody today, but it will put the wrong classification on a notification and it leaves the crew without the test that actually applies to the person on the floor.
blocking.fix: Replace the final sentence of the fall paragraph with: "Notification: if the fall injured the person, it is notifiable as a serious injury or illness under Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Qld) s 36 — immediate treatment as an in-patient in a hospital, or immediate treatment for a serious head or spinal injury, a serious burn, an amputation, loss of a bodily function or serious lacerations — which makes it a notifiable incident under s 35. Section 37(f), the fall or release from a height of any plant, substance or thing, is the paragraph for a dropped drill, core barrel or core plug, not for the person. Either way, call WHSQ on 1300 362 128 immediately by the fastest possible means (s 38) and leave the plant and the scene as they are (s 39)."

blocking.problem: steps[1].controls[1] is the visual tells list — "6 mm compressed sheet with a dimpled or brushed face, Super Six corrugated, tapered eaves sheeting, textured vermiculite ceilings, millboard behind heaters, Zelemite or Ausbestos switchboard panels, rope gasket in a fire door or damper" — and it omits two of the five hazards named in its own step. steps[1].hazards[2] is "Vinyl floor tile and its black bitumen adhesive where you core the floor for pipework" and steps[1].hazards[3] is "Friable pipe lagging in the riser you are drilling beside"; neither appears in the tells. Vinyl tile and its bitumen backing and adhesive are among the most commonly missed ACM in commercial buildings and are routinely absent from registers, and they are directly in the path of the floor coring this SWMS covers.
blocking.fix: Append to steps[1].controls[1]: "...9 in. or 12 in. vinyl floor tile and the black bitumen backing and adhesive under it — including under later vinyl or carpet, which is exactly what you core through for floor pipework — and pipe, boiler or duct lagging, hard-set or fabric-wrapped, anywhere in the riser or plant room you are working in."

blocking.problem: steps[3].controls[0] ends: "If the site will not isolate, the work does not proceed on a locator and a depth stop unless the Safe QLD supervisor authorises it in writing, on the day, on this SWMS — and in that case the residual risk for this step is HIGH, not medium, and you work it that way." But steps[3].residualRisk is already "high". The escalation therefore does nothing: whether the circuit is isolated and proven dead or the crew is drilling on a locator and a depth stop with a written supervisor authorisation, the statement shows the same rating. The one signal the document has for telling the crew that today is the worse of the two cases is inert, and the crew cannot tell from the step which case they are working in. Nobody is under-warned by this — high is the conservative rating — but the control loses its force, and by the document's own rule ("If the controls in a step are not all in place on the day, the residual reverts to the initial rating and you stop") the un-isolated case is arguably extreme, not high.
blocking.fix: Set steps[3].residualRisk to "medium" for the isolated case, which is what steps[3].controls[0] plainly assumes, and amend that control to close: "...and in that case the residual risk for this step is HIGH, not medium — write HIGH on the signed copy, brief it at the toolbox, and work it that way: nobody else in the drill zone, one hole at a time, and the tool comes out at the depth stop." If the intended reading is instead that this step is high in every case, delete the words "not medium" and replace them with "the same as it is with isolation, because a locator is not a control — which is why this is the one case that needs the supervisor's name on it."
